title: Study Abroad Report: Duke University
paragraphs: Through the Nagoya University exchange program, I studied abroad at Duke University for three months. Some of you may already know that Duke University is the central presence in the city of Durham, North Carolina, in the United States. The Durham campus is lush with trees, and I often saw small birds and animals such as squirrels, in a very green country town. In that peaceful town, a turbulent life abroad unlike anything I had ever experienced began. To begin with, I am not a returnee from overseas, nor am I fluent in English. What made someone like me decide to take on studying abroad was the encouragement of my mentor.
"The world is wide. For young people like you, feeling the world while you are young will be a great asset."

I had been taking part in a study group run by Professor 長谷川 of respiratory medicine, and it was there that I became interested in studying abroad. Once it was decided, I set off for Duke University with half interest and half anxiety.

During the three months I was able to do clerkships at Duke University Hospital in pulmonary medicine, neurology, neuroradiology and cardiology, together with local students and exchange students from various countries.

In the clerkships in the United States you can have experiences that are not possible in the polyclinic clerkships in Japan. But the flip side is that you have to do things you have never done before in English, which is not your native language, so at first I felt a very large wall. Although medical students in the United States do not have a medical license, I felt that they are treated as Drs. among the staff of the medical team. This probably means that medical students have won great trust in the hospital and that they bear a responsibility commensurate with it. For that reason, you are corrected for unprofessional attitudes, such as leaving something you do not understand as it is, or when a team member knows your own patient better than you do. Through such clerkships, I think I was able to acquire not only knowledge but also a mental foundation of awareness and responsibility as a physician.

Now, as for the actual content of the clerkship, first we do rounding as a team from around 7 in the morning. Before then I would already have seen my own patients, and at rounding I report on my patients' condition to the senior physician. In between, I handle consult patients requested by other departments. The first touch of patients consulted from other departments is done by students. After checking the chart, the student goes to the patient, takes the history while listening to them, and performs the necessary physical examination. After the examination, I make my own differential diagnosis and diagnose. I report on the patient to the senior physician and also propose the tests and treatments the patient needs in response to my own diagnosis. A patient I handled in this way remains my patient until transfer to another department or discharge, and I continue to follow up afterward. I was able to experience evaluating a patient from scratch, thinking it through and deciding the treatment plan, and I felt that learning and growing in it was a great pleasure. I was able to experience firsthand the strengths of American medical education. When making such a proposal, you are required to present solid evidence while citing papers. For that reason, the habit of searching for various articles on my own took hold, and I felt that the barrier between clinical practice and research became considerably lower in me.

Now, the pulmonary medicine department at Duke actively performs lung transplants, and I could see them being applied to a wide range of diseases, such as sarcoidosis, pulmonary fibrosis and cystic fibrosis, which is hardly seen in Japan. I had the opportunity to be in charge of a patient who had received a lung transplant, and I was greatly struck by the dramatic improvement in lung function. Dr. Tapson, the attending who guided me for one month in pulmonary medicine, is a specialist in pulmonary hypertension and puts great effort into clinical research too, and in the clerkship he taught me how to build research on the basis of clinical experience.

Through this study abroad I was able to gain much life experience in addition to the clerkship. This time I left Japan for my first long stay overseas. In the course of it I was able to deepen my reflection on the cultures and medical circumstances of Japan and the United States, and I think I became able, if anything, to evaluate Japan more objectively. In addition, Duke University has local students and excellent exchange students from all over the world. Working and learning with them was very stimulating and made me grow. In the future I would very much like to have another opportunity to work with them, and I want to grow so that we can both spend stimulating time then. On days off, I was also invited by senior doctors called attendings to their laboratories and to parties at their homes. On such occasions I was able to interact with people who are "first-class" in their field, whether in research or in clinical practice. I came to know many career paths as a physician, and I could once again feel the profession of physician to be interesting and something to be proud of.

Through this experience, I was able to learn how to keep growing as a physician and how to enjoy it. Honestly, I was bewildered by communicating in English at first, but I was given far more valuable experiences than that. I express my gratitude to Dr. 伊藤, Dr. 坂本, Dr. 粕谷 and Ms. 平光 of the International Exchange Office and everyone in the academic affairs office who cooperated with my study abroad, to Dr. 長谷川 who gave me the opportunity to study abroad, to my classmates and seniors who helped me from the pre-departure training sessions through the time abroad, to the doctors at Duke and my host family who looked after me during the clerkship, and to my family who kept cheering on my challenge from Japan. I think the greatest way to repay them is to become a physician and grow from now on, using this valuable experience as nourishment, so I will continue to work even harder.
I would be very happy if, by passing on this wonderful experience to the juniors, the exchange program and this Frontier Society become ever more fruitful. Thank you very much.
